name: Anastrozole

lead: Anastrozole is a prescription aromatase inhibitor approved for breast cancer in postmenopausal women. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed for delaying growth-plate closure to add adult height, and by TRT users for keeping oestrogen low.

It blocks aromatase, the enzyme that converts testosterone and androstenedione to oestrogen, lowering oestradiol. Oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, which is the basis of the height interest. No controlled trial shows a height gain in healthy adolescents, and a 2023 gynecomastia review says it has not been consistently useful in boys.

paras: Heightmaxxers discuss it alongside growth hormone and similar compounds, while TRT users discuss it as part of oestrogen management. It is prescription-only, and height use is off-label.

The label lists reduced bone density, higher cholesterol, cardiovascular events in women with heart disease and fetal harm. Forum users report fatigue and crashed oestrogen. Use for height in adolescents is off-label and untested.

social.title: Anastrozole: Thousands to be offered drug to prevent breast cancer in England

angle.text: Anastrozole lowers oestrogen, and since oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, teen heightmaxxers hope it keeps plates open for extra adult height; TRT users use it for oestrogen control. Its approved use is breast cancer, and the height idea has not been tested in healthy people.

lead: Anastrozole, sold as Arimidex among other brands, is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor taken by mouth. It blocks the enzyme that converts androgens such as testosterone and androstenedione into oestrogens, and it is approved for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women.[1][2][3][4] In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding settings it is discussed for three appearance goals: keeping oestrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia (breast tissue in males) and water retention in check during testosterone use, easing the way toward a leaner-looking physique, and, among younger users, delaying growth-plate closure in the hope of a taller adult height.[5][6][7][8]

Oestrogen is the hormone that drives growth plates to fuse at the end of puberty in both sexes, which is the reasoning behind the height interest: proponents argue that lowering oestrogen extends the window in which bones can lengthen, usually alongside growth hormone or a secretagogue.[5][6][7][9] Aromatase inhibitors have been studied in clinical settings for delayed puberty and short stature in boys, and anastrozole is used for some forms of precocious puberty in boys,[4][10][1] but published trials in healthy adolescents seeking extra height were not found. A 2023 review of gynecomastia in boys notes that tamoxifen has been tried successfully in adolescents while anastrozole and letrozole have not been consistently useful.[11]

The US label documents reduced bone mineral density, raised cholesterol, ischaemic cardiovascular events in women with existing heart disease and possible fetal harm.[3] Anastrozole is prescription-only in the US, Canada, UK and Australia, and use for height or physique goals is off-label; for adolescents it is not an approved indication.[4][3]
infobox: Patented by Imperial Chemical Industries 1987; approved for medical use 1995[4]
Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women[3]

paras: The US label lists adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer in postmenopausal women, first-line treatment of locally advanced or metastatic disease, and treatment of advanced disease that has progressed after tamoxifen.[3] The ATAC trial and other randomised trials compared anastrozole with tamoxifen in this setting,[12][13][14][15] and a switching trial (ABCSG 8 and ARNO 95) examined moving women to anastrozole after two years of tamoxifen.[16] A 2010 review summarises its pharmacology and comparative efficacy and safety against tamoxifen.[17]

Beyond cancer, anastrozole has been used off-label for breast-cancer risk reduction in high-risk postmenopausal women and, together with an anti-androgen, for peripheral precocious puberty in boys such as in McCune-Albright syndrome.[1][4] It has also been studied as a way of raising testosterone in men with hypogonadism, with long-term bone effects noted as a concern.[4]

Appearance-related interest centres on three ideas. The first is height: delaying skeletal maturation by lowering oestrogen, which forum users pair with growth hormone or MK-677.[5][6][7][9] The second is oestrogen control during testosterone or anabolic use, to limit gynecomastia, water retention and puffy-looking tissue; this is the use discussed on T Nation, where men on testosterone replacement describe adding anastrozole to bring oestradiol into range.[18][19][20] The third, on looksmax.org, is a hoped-for leaner body composition, with one 15-year-old poster saying he understood aromatase inhibitors could help him lose fat.[5][8]

Gynecomastia treatment is a recognised appearance-linked medical use of the drug class. Reference sources describe tamoxifen as the most effective medical option and anastrozole as an off-label choice, mainly for pubertal cases, that is generally less effective than tamoxifen; surgery is used for persistent cases.[21][11]

Anastrozole was patented by Imperial Chemical Industries in 1987 and approved for medical use in 1995 for breast cancer; it later became a generic drug and is on the World Health Organization List of Essential Medicines.[4] It belongs to the third-generation aromatase inhibitors, alongside letrozole and the steroidal inhibitor exemestane.[17][10]

The pivotal data came from the ATAC trial, which randomised more than 9,000 postmenopausal women to anastrozole, tamoxifen or both; first results appeared in 2002 and follow-up analyses at five, about eight and ten years reported better disease-free survival with anastrozole than with tamoxifen.[12][14][15][13] In 2023 England announced plans to offer anastrozole to high-risk women for breast-cancer prevention, a development discussed on Hacker News.[22]

Its entry into appearance culture came through two channels: bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy communities, where oestrogen management became a routine topic, and later heightmaxxing forums, where teenagers began discussing aromatase inhibitors as an extension of growth-hormone use.[6][7][23][18]

Anastrozole binds reversibly to aromatase and competes with its androgen substrates, so oestrogen production in peripheral tissues falls.[4][10] The US label states that it significantly lowers serum oestradiol.[3] Reference sources report aromatase inhibition of roughly 97 per cent at the standard tablet strength and oestradiol reductions of at least 85 per cent in postmenopausal women.[4] The steroidal inhibitor exemestane, by contrast, binds the enzyme irreversibly; forum users contrast the two, saying anastrozole crosses the blood-brain barrier less and has fewer androgenic effects.[10][9]

Peak blood levels occur at around three hours, steady state is reached in 7 to 10 days, and the half-life is about 40 to 50 hours; most of the drug is cleared by the liver.[4] It has negligible effects on major cytochrome P450 enzymes, so interactions with other drugs are uncommon.[4]

Label warnings include increased ischaemic cardiovascular events compared with tamoxifen in women with pre-existing ischaemic heart disease, decreases in bone mineral density, increased total cholesterol, and embryo-fetal toxicity.[3] Common effects listed in reference sources include hot flushes, fatigue, joint pain, mood changes, nausea, headache and insomnia; rare serious reactions include skin lesions, allergic reactions and liver abnormalities.[4][3] A review of the drug's safety profile reports similar themes in postmenopausal women.[17]

Aromatase inhibitors are linked to bone loss and joint symptoms in women; reference sources say men do not appear to show the same bone harms, although the evidence on long-term use in men is limited.[10][4] Oestrogen also supports bone density in adolescents, which is why bone effects are discussed in connection with use in teens; trials in healthy adolescents have not been published.

Users themselves describe over-suppression. A looksmax.org poster says that taken without exogenous testosterone the result is lowered oestrogen and bone loss, and another says long-term use makes a person lazy and slow.[5][8] On T Nation, men report low libido, a soft feeling or fatigue when oestradiol is pushed too low, and one thread is devoted to a user who found even a small dose too much.[24][25][19]

The evidence base is overwhelmingly in breast cancer: the ATAC trial (anastrozole versus tamoxifen, alone or combined),[12][14][15][13] a North American first-line trial,[26] the ABCSG 8 and ARNO 95 switching analysis,[16] and combination trials with CDK4/6 inhibitors such as ribociclib and abemaciclib.[27][28][29] A 10-year ATAC analysis and subsequent work reported lower recurrence with anastrozole than tamoxifen in hormone receptor-positive disease.[13]

Registered studies in other groups include bioavailability studies in healthy volunteers, a gynecomastia extension study, a trial in McCune-Albright syndrome and a trial in elderly hypogonadal men.[30][31][32] No published randomised trial in healthy adolescents has tested anastrozole to increase adult height. Reviews of aromatase inhibitors list experimental work in delayed puberty and idiopathic short stature in boys, and a 2023 paediatric review says anastrozole and letrozole have not been consistently useful for gynecomastia in this age group.[10][11]

Anastrozole is prescription-only in the US, Canada, UK and Australia, and is marketed under Arimidex and many generic names.[4][3] Forum threads show users, including self-described minors, asking how to obtain it without a prescription; these are posts, not endorsements of any route.[6][7][33]

Many looksmax.org threads, several started by people who describe themselves as 13 to 16 years old, ask which aromatase inhibitor to use for height, how it pairs with growth hormone or MK-677, and where to obtain it.[6][7][9][23][33] A recurring comparison is anastrozole versus exemestane (Aromasin): one poster says exemestane raises androgens and has fewer bone effects, while a reply says a non-steroidal inhibitor is the better pick.[9]

Some replies caution against it. One answers that they would not use an aromatase inhibitor in the first place, and a thread titled with a warning advises against aromatase inhibitors outright.[5][34] Others say it should be used only guided by bloodwork and typically alongside exogenous testosterone.[8]

On T Nation, men on testosterone replacement discuss adding anastrozole to manage oestradiol, debate whether it is needed at all, and report mixed experiences, from improved erectile function and less lethargy to fatigue and low libido attributed to too much oestrogen suppression.[18][19][24][25]

lore.intro: Anastrozole is discussed mostly as a heightmaxxing and oestrogen-control drug, frequently by teenagers on looksmax.org and by adult testosterone users on T Nation, and users debate it against exemestane and letrozole.[5][6][9][18]

North American trial reports anastrozole superior to tamoxifen as first-line therapy in advanced disease.[26]
First results of the ATAC trial published.[12]
Five-year ATAC results and the ABCSG 8 / ARNO 95 switching analysis reported.[14][16]
Long T Nation threads discuss anastrozole alongside testosterone replacement and hCG.[19][18][20]
England announces plans to offer anastrozole for breast-cancer prevention; a review of paediatric gynecomastia notes inconsistent usefulness of anastrozole in boys.[22][11]
